extracted.intended_audience: Citizens of New York / politically engaged public considering the proposed U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance on allocating powers to a national senate (treaty-making, appointments, impeachment trials) and on institutional features (selection method, tenure, secrecy, checks) to secure competent, stable, and accountable government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate composition and mode of election
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate should be elected indirectly by the people (via state legislatures or select bodies) and not be confined to particular families or fortunes; staggered terms and rotation prevent consolidation of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: indirect election and composition by enlightened/select bodies lead to appointments of 'men...distinguished by their abilities and virtue'; Maryland's indirectly-elected Senate (with similar features) shows no symptoms of aristocratic usurpation; historical examples (Britain, Sparta, Rome, Carthage) indicate that popular branches generally check senatorial bodies. Beware claims that an indirectly-elected Senate necessarily produces aristocracy — experience and comparison rebut that fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection by select electors/state legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing presidents by select electors and senators by state legislatures ensures appointments by bodies 'composed of the most enlightened and respectable citizens' who can gather extensive information on candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mode 'vastly' advantages over popular elections that may be swayed by party zeal, supineness, ignorance, or fleeting appearances of genius; select bodies are presumed to pick men 'who best understand our national interests' and 'whose reputation for integrity inspires and merits confidence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and qualification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional age limits (excluding men under 35 for the first office and under 30 for the second) confine offices to persons the people have had time to judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: prevents election of those dazzled by 'brilliant appearances' and ensures electors choose persons with established character and abilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure/duration in office for competence and continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer duration in office for senators provides time to acquire exact information, political experience, and to form/steward systems of national affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staggered/rotating elections preserve 'a considerable residue of the old ones in place' to maintain uniformity, order, and a continual succession of official information; this counters the inconvenience of transferring important affairs entirely to new men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty-making: combined deliberation and rapidity
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of making treaties should be exercised by the President 'by and with the advice and consent of the Senate' (two-thirds concurrence), combining the advantages of concentrated executive action and senatorial deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaty negotiations often require both 'talents, information, integrity, and deliberate investigations' and 'perfect secrecy and immediate despatch.' Vesting treaty power in the executive with senatorial consent preserves secrecy/despatch while ensuring deliberative check and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy and despatch as criteria for allocating powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain negotiations demand perfect secrecy and immediate despatch; bodies that cannot reliably provide secrecy or rapid action are less fit for such duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large popular assemblies are less trustworthy for secrecy; the President can manage intelligence and urgent opportunities (e.g., battles, deaths, ministerial changes) more effectively and can convene the Senate when their advice/consent is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaties should have stable, binding legal effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Treaties are bargains between nations and should be 'the SUPREME laws of the land,' not subject to unilateral repeal by domestic legislatures without the co-operation of the other contracting party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If treaties were treated as repealable at pleasure by one party, foreign nations would refuse to enter binding bargains; treaties must be regarded as binding to maintain international credit and reciprocal obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal state representation as protection of state interests
rubrics_metrics.description: As all States are equally represented in the Senate, each will have an equal degree of influence, especially if they appoint proper persons and insist on punctual attendance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equality helps ensure the national government considers the good of each part; as the Union becomes more national, the good of the whole aligns with the good of each state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability standards and remedies for corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Those entrusted with treaty-making and other powers should be restrained by motives like honor, oaths, reputation, conscience, love of country and family, and by constitutional mechanisms such as impeachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corruption is deemed unlikely given human incentives and selection safeguards; fraudulent treaties would be 'null and void by the law of nations'; impeachment provisions add further security for fidelity and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate tribunal for impeachment trials
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate, as a numerous, dignified, and (relatively) independent body, is the most fit tribunal for trying impeachments — a national inquest into the conduct of public men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: the Senate can be impartial between accused individuals and their accusers (the people's representatives); it is numerous enough to exercise awful discretion without unduly concentrating power; it enjoys credibility and authority necessary to reconcile people to difficult decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding conflation of ordinary judiciary with impeachment function
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court would be an improper substitute for the Senate as a court of impeachments because its members are too few, may lack requisite fortitude, and combining the functions would risk prejudicing subsequent criminal trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making the same persons judges in both impeachment and criminal proceedings could deprive accused persons of the protections of a double trial; the plan's compromise is to have the Chief Justice preside over Senate impeachment trials to obtain some benefits of judicial participation without full union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible partial intermixture of powers for specific purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Separation of powers need not be absolute; a partial intermixture (e.g., legislative participation in impeachment trials, executive check on legislation) is compatible with preserving departments 'distinct and unconnected' in the main and may be necessary for mutual defense among branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: legislative negative on executive acts, senate's role in treaties and appointments are forms of necessary checks; the maxim of separation should be understood as flexible for practical government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment court composition trade-offs (permanent separate court vs Senate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing a wholly distinct, permanent impeachment court is problematic because it would be expensive or logistically cumbersome (calling state officers); both permanent and ad hoc alternatives have serious practical drawbacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanent officers would be costly and stationary; calling dispersed state officers causes delay, inconvenience, and opportunities for corruption or inaction that harm the public; hence the Senate is a practical and prudent choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterpoises between legislative branches
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific powers assigned to the House (origination of money bills, sole right to institute impeachments, deciding the presidential election in certain cases) serve as important counterbalances to Senate authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exclusive authorities ensure the popular branch retains potent checks (especially over finance and initiation of impeachments) and help prevent the Senate from becoming predominant or aristocratic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of practical governmental function over theoretical perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution should not be rejected because particular provisions are not the best imaginable; the standard is whether the plan is good and practicable overall, not whether every part attains an exact standard of perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding out for an infallible design would lead to anarchy; reasonable compromises and pragmatic arrangements that secure overall good should be accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for steady, carefully formed policy in commerce and navigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Affairs of trade and navigation demand a cautiously formed and steadily pursued system; both treaties and laws should correspond and be made to promote these objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who deny the need for steady systems underestimate national needs; entrusting treaty and law concurrence to capable bodies (President+Senate) helps maintain necessary correspondence for economic policy.
